title: Biology offers design principles for unstructured environments
source: Research objectives; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk
notes: Our first goal is more capable autonomous robots in unstructured environments. Wheels remain efficient on prepared warehouse floors. Sand, forests, and rubble motivate legs, compliant actuation, and sensory neural control. Elastic energy recovery and efficient control are design motivations, not energy savings demonstrated by this dissertation. We therefore need to know whether our chosen biological analogues actually supply the intended capabilities.Sources: Ben’s research-goal directive; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk

title: Biomimetic robots can also test biological hypotheses
source: Research objectives; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk
notes: The second goal runs in the other direction. Biological knowledge informs robots, and increasingly biomimetic robots provide experimental access to mechanics and neural pathways. We can change a route or remove a feedback pathway and measure the consequence under repeatable conditions. Such interventions can be impossible or inappropriate in human subjects. Better prosthetic and orthotic devices are a tertiary application of the resulting understanding. The robot must first be characterized well enough that an effect can be interpreted.Sources: Ben’s research-goal directive; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk

title: Four knowledge gaps organize this dissertation
source: Research objectives; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk
notes: The research goals require four foundations. First, predict artificial-muscle force when actuator length changes. Second, predict what torque the real transmission delivers and compare it with the intended human-muscle target. Third, locate sensory evidence with its experimental context. Fourth, build tools that make coupled circuit behavior testable. These are the four sections of this talk. A general background section is unnecessary; introduce each concept where its question arises.Sources: Ben’s research-goal directive; Dissertation Ch. 1; older Movement and Control talk

title: The walker attempts exposed a need for interpretable model tests
source: Dissertation Ch. 6, opening narrative and tools gap
notes: The Li–Deng/W2L work combines published mechanics and a layered neural controller. Suspended motion did not automatically transfer to supported or weight-bearing behavior, and the MATLAB/Simulink implementation raised additional questions about implementation and coupling. A failed or rhythmic trajectory alone could not identify the cause. I therefore developed a workflow for checking the circuit, connecting actuators and sensors, tuning in stages, and changing one condition at a time. The demonstrations that follow answer distinct questions within that workflow.Sources: Dissertation Ch. 6, opening narrative and tools gaprobot

title: Two deleted bursts can preserve or reset the rhythm
source: Dissertation Ch. 6 and Appendix D · Current saved verification records
notes: The reduced Deng-derived translated circuit is coupled to a suspended model. Stimuli lasting two baseline periods suppress two expected flexor motor bursts at each tested layer. RG-extensor +50 nA shifts both RG and motor timing by 0.211 cycle. PF-extensor +50 nA suppresses output without resetting the RG clock, and flexor-MN −500 nA also gives a non-resetting deletion. Read left RG traces and right MN activation together. Stronger-current controls matter: a one-second PF pulse shifts motor timing by 0.208 cycle while RG timing stays unchanged. A motor shift alone therefore does not prove RG resetting. This is a translated reduced-circuit test, not original-rat locomotion replication.Sources: Dissertation Ch. 6 and Appendix D · Current saved verification recordslayers

title: These contributions enable better-defined research experiments
source: Dissertation Introduction, Discussion, and Conclusion
notes: Return to our research goals. The force model supports actuator choice; joint factors support interpreting the transmission; SADb supports selecting a sensory hypothesis; and the SNS tools support controlled interventions. A researcher can now separate a force-capacity question from a pathway-sign question or a model-coupling fault. This is how the contributions advance the robot as an experimental instrument, while autonomous behavior remains an integration goal.Sources: Dissertation Introduction, Discussion, and Conclusion

title: Future experiments can connect these foundations to the research goals
source: Dissertation Discussion; current model limitations
notes: Organize future work by the original goals rather than by a software to-do list. For autonomous robots, test dynamic actuator/transmission behavior, effective neural control, and progressive support reduction under explicit gait criteria. For biological understanding, compare controlled pathway and mechanical changes with experimental response signatures. Prosthetic and orthotic studies are a later translation requiring task-specific and human validation. The immediate work is to establish the validity and interpretation of each experiment.Sources: Dissertation Discussion; current model limitations

title: The dissertation makes key biomimetic design assumptions testable
source: Ben P. Bolen · Portland State University · AARL
notes: Conclude the argument. Our long-term goals are capable autonomous robots and biological insight, with assistive devices as a further application. This dissertation supplies resting-length-aware force prediction, corrected and physically tested knee routes, source-linked sensory evidence, and tools for controlled neuromechanical experiments. All nine extensor and fifteen flexor measurements meet the selected human-muscle targets. These foundations enable stronger experiments; they do not by themselves establish an autonomous walking humanoid. Thank the advisor, committee, AARL, and collaborators, then invite questions.Sources: Ben P. Bolen · Portland State University · AARL
